strengths: The core insight is interesting and well-motivated: the paper shows that per-token cosine similarity across adjacent layers (the assumption underlying MiniCache) is low, while CKA analysis reveals that dominant singular vectors/bases of KV-caches are well aligned across layers. This reframing motivates cross-layer SVD and is supported by a clear appendix derivation connecting CKA to aligned left singular vectors.

The method (xKV) is simple, plug-and-play, and technically sound: SVD over horizontally concatenated caches of grouped adjacent layers yields a shared token basis A plus layer-specific reconstruction matrices B, with no retraining or architectural change needed.

Empirical results are strong: at ~8x compression on RULER (64K context), xKV-4 retains 87-88% average accuracy where Single SVD collapses (~24-35%) and MiniCache collapses at even 1.3x. Results are consistent across three GQA models and also hold on the MLA-based DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite (~3x on top of MLA), which demonstrates generality across attention variants.

The ablations (key vs. value compressibility, group size 2 vs. 4, per-task behavior in Figure 5) and the honest limitations section (fixed rank allocation, lack of end-to-end system/throughput demonstration) are appropriate and add credibility.

Practical deployment details are thoughtfully addressed: on-the-fly SVD during prefill, pre-RoPE key decomposition with re-rotation, leaving newly generated tokens uncompressed, and MLA-specific treatment of decoupled RoPE keys.
weaknesses: Baseline coverage is narrow. Comparisons are limited to MiniCache and a per-layer Single SVD. Other directly relevant low-rank KV-compression baselines that the paper itself cites (Palu, EigenAttention, LoRC, ShadowKV) are not compared, making it hard to judge xKV's advantage over the broader state of the art rather than a deliberately weak set of baselines.

The headline claim 'up to 6.8x higher compression rates than SOTA inter-layer technique while improving accuracy by 2.7%' is framed favorably: MiniCache's maximum usable rate is only 1.3x, and the comparison is against the authors' own reimplementation ('code for MiniCache was not publicly available'), which raises questions about whether the reimplemented baseline was optimally tuned.

Evaluation scope is limited: a single context length (64K) on RULER, one additional task family (coding) for MLA, and no error bars/multiple seeds. Accuracy still degrades noticeably at 8x (e.g., 70.9 vs 92.0 on Llama-3.1-8B), so 'lossless' holds only at ~2.4x, and no wall-clock latency/throughput or real memory measurements are provided (the <10% prefill overhead figure is asserted without details).

The theoretical link between shared-subspace SVD error and end-task accuracy is absent; the method's justification is purely empirical (eigenvalue analysis on one model, Llama-3.1-8B, on one NIAH dataset). It remains unexplained why grouping helps at fixed overall compression despite reducing per-layer rank headroom.

Practical memory/latency costs of the on-the-fly grouped SVD are under-analyzed: materializing concatenated caches for a group before decomposition could inflate peak prefill memory, and reconstruction matmuls add decode-time FLOPs; neither is measured in a system context.
Reproducibility concerns: the code URL in the abstract appears empty/broken ('available at: .'), and the CKA/eigenvalue motivating analyses are presented only for a single model/dataset.

strengths: The core observation is interesting and well-motivated: the CKA analysis (Figure 2b) showing that adjacent layers have low token-wise cosine similarity but well-aligned dominant singular vectors is a genuinely useful reframing of prior cross-layer merging assumptions (e.g., MiniCache's SLERP), and the Appendix A derivation linking CKA to left-singular-vector overlap is correct and clarifies why low-rank cross-layer sharing should work.

The method itself is simple and plug-and-play: a single SVD on horizontally concatenated KV-caches of grouped layers, with layer-specific reconstruction matrices, requiring no retraining or architectural changes. Figure 1 and Table 1 show convincing gains over both Single SVD and MiniCache at 2.4x–8x compression on three GQA models, and the Qwen2.5-7B (4 KV heads) result suggests the effect is not an artifact of one model family.
The paper is transparent about limitations (fixed rank allocation, no end-to-end system evaluation) and reasonably honest that generated tokens are left uncompressed, following prior work.
Compatibility with MLA (DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite) and pre-RoPE key decomposition shows the authors thought about practical integration details across attention variants.
weaknesses: The evaluation is narrow for the claims made. The main benchmark (RULER) consists largely of synthetic retrieval-style tasks at a single context length (64K), yet the paper repeatedly positions xKV for 'long-context inference' at 128K/1M scales. No natural long-context evaluation (e.g., other LongBench tasks, narrative QA, book-length summarization) is provided for the GQA models, and the Rank Ratio analysis (Figure 2c) is based on a single NIAH dataset on a single model, leaving the generality of the motivating observation under-supported.

No comparison against any baseline outside the inter-layer/low-rank family. Quantization (KIVI, KVQuant), token eviction (H2O, SnapKV, PyramidKV), and low-rank projection methods (Palu, LoRC) are all cited but never compared, even though these are the standard competitive baselines and are orthogonal/combinable. It is impossible to judge whether cross-layer SVD is a better use of memory than, e.g., 4-bit quantization at the same effective footprint.

Reproducibility claim is contradicted by the manuscript itself: the abstract's code link is empty ('Our code is publicly available at: .'). Additionally, MiniCache is re-implemented by the authors rather than run from official code, and MiniCache's compression range (1.1x–1.3x) is far below where xKV operates; the headline '6.8x higher compression than the state-of-the-art inter-layer technique' compares xKV's operating point to MiniCache's degradation point rather than a matched-accuracy comparison, which reads as oversold.

The method has a practical cost that is only partially addressed: cross-layer SVD must be performed on the fly during prefill for every request, and the reconstruction matmul A*B is paid at every decode step for every layer. The paper reports <10% prefill overhead at 128K but provides no end-to-end latency, throughput, or measured memory numbers at all — the entire evaluation is accuracy-only. For a systems-motivated contribution, this is a significant evidential gap, acknowledged but not resolved in Section 6.

Several design choices appear tuned rather than justified: the 1:1.5 key/value rank ratio, the stride-based grouping (why contiguous groups rather than the CKA-optimal grouping the analysis would suggest?), and the fixed rank allocation are all asserted without ablation. The gap between xKV-2 and xKV-4 at 8x compression on Qwen2.5-7B (64.0 vs 78.1 average) shows sensitivity to grouping that is not analyzed.

Presentation issues undermine confidence: repeated citation errors (RepoBench-P attributed to '[8, 33]' when [8] is LongBench; ShadowKV's arXiv number belongs to ShadowLLM in [5]), typos ('by and constructing', 'grouped of layers', 'exploits' vs 'exploit'), and the missing code link noted above. Individually minor, collectively they suggest the paper was not carefully finalized.

The MLA experiment (Figure 4) covers only two coding tasks with a small model (2.4B activated parameters), and the claim of '3x compression without performance degradation' is shown only as a plot without the numerical detail given to RULER.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated core insight: the paper distinguishes token-wise cosine similarity (low across layers, which limits MiniCache) from CKA-based singular-vector alignment (high across layers), and Appendix A gives a reasonable derivation connecting high CKA to aligned dominant left singular vectors. This is a genuine understanding contribution beyond simply applying SVD.

The proposed method (xKV) is simple, plug-and-play, requires no retraining or architectural change, and the horizontal-concatenation SVD with shared basis A and layer-specific reconstruction matrices B is clearly described and easy to reproduce in spirit.

Empirically strong results: on RULER at 64K across Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Qwen2.5-14B, xKV substantially outperforms both Single SVD (its own ablation at matched compression) and a re-implemented MiniCache, e.g., 87.8 avg accuracy at ~8× compression vs 35.3 for Single SVD on Llama-3.1-8B. The observation that larger groups (xKV-4) dominate at matched compression directly supports the cross-layer sharing hypothesis.

Useful generality check: demonstrating further compression on DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite's already low-rank MLA latent cache (~3× on coding tasks with no degradation) shows the method applies to emerging architectures, not just GQA models.
Honest limitations section identifying fixed rank allocation and the absence of end-to-end system (throughput/latency) measurements, and the prefill-time overhead (<10% at 128K) is quantified.
weaknesses: Baseline coverage is narrow. The only inter-layer comparison is MiniCache, which was re-implemented because official code was unavailable, and is driven to failure at only ~1.3× compression; the original MiniCache paper reports higher usable compression, so the 'up to 6.8× higher compression than SOTA' headline claim rests on a possibly unflattering reimplementation. No comparison against other low-rank post-training methods (Palu, LoRC, EigenAttention, ShadowKV-style hybrid SVD+sparse) at matched compression, so it is hard to situate xKV against the broader state of the art.

No end-to-end system evaluation. The method stores A, B matrices and performs reconstruction matmuls during decode; decoding speed, throughput, and realized memory savings are unmeasured. For a systems-motivated contribution, accuracy-vs-compression curves alone leave the central practical claim (addressing the memory bottleneck) only partially supported, even though the authors acknowledge this.

Evaluation breadth is limited: RULER at a single context length (64K) plus two coding tasks on one model. No standard general-capability or long-generation evaluation, and the interaction with quantization/token eviction (obvious complements) is unexplored.

The core claims are empirical heuristics without quantitative justification. CKA is shown high for some layer pairs, but there is no analysis of how CKA relates to actual reconstruction/accuracy loss, no error bound for the shared-basis approximation, and no justification beyond convention for the fixed 1:1.5 key/value rank ratio or for stride-based (rather than CKA-guided) grouping; Figure 2b shows substantial layer-pair variation that the grouping strategy ignores.

Compression-rate accounting is somewhat opaque: rates are computed assuming a 64K context with generated tokens left uncompressed, and pre-RoPE decomposition details complicate direct comparison; per-figure compression axes (e.g., 8.4× vs 8.0×) are not fully explained.

Presentation and reproducibility issues: the code URL in the abstract is blank, there are multiple typos (e.g., 'Mixter-of-Experts', 'by and constructing'), and MiniCache's reimplementation setup differs from its original reported configuration, weakening reproducibility of the comparisons.

strengths: The motivating analysis is genuinely informative: the paper clearly distinguishes token-wise cosine similarity (low across layers) from structural alignment measured by CKA (high across layers), and supports the compression hypothesis with a rank-vs-grouping spectral analysis (Figure 2c). The Appendix A derivation connecting CKA to dominant left singular vector alignment is a useful, correct contribution.

The proposed method (cross-layer factorization via SVD with a shared token basis) is simple, training-free, and well-motivated, and the Selective Reconstruction (SR) extension is a sensible way to avoid the O(L) dense reconstruction bottleneck by building on the ShadowKV-style landmark pipeline.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: RULER at 64K and 122K, multi-turn NIAH, LongBench, three GQA models plus MLA (DeepSeek) and hybrid attention (GPT-OSS) in the appendix, and a broad set of baselines (quantization, eviction, low-rank, token selection, inter-layer merging) with generally matched or favorable compression rates.

Headline results are strong and consistent: ~8x compression with only 2-3% average accuracy loss on RULER, clear wins over MiniCache and Single-SVD, robustness in multi-turn settings where eviction methods collapse, and end-to-end throughput gains (up to 4.23x) for xKV-SR that are backed by attention latency measurements.

Good ablation coverage: window size (Table 8), key-vs-value compressibility (Figure 6, D.3), integration with quantization (D.5), on-the-fly SVD overhead (C.1), and FLOP/memory accounting (D.6) make the cost model transparent. Code is stated to be publicly available, and the limitations section honestly identifies the long-generation setting as out of scope.

Notable system insight: xKV-SR achieves enough fidelity to keep compressed keys and values entirely on GPU, eliminating the PCIe offloading bottleneck that constrains ShadowKV, which explains the measured throughput advantage rather than just accuracy improvements.
weaknesses: Numerical inconsistencies between text and tables undermine confidence in reporting: C.1 states 'approx. 3.9% of prefill time at 128K' and '3.17% at 64k' on an A6000, but Table 3 (A100) shows 2.50% at 128k and 5.72% at 64k; Table 1 is introduced for 'Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M' but the table header reads Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-1M; Full Attn baselines differ slightly between Tables 1 and 9 (91.89 vs 92.09) without explanation. None of these change conclusions, but they should be corrected.

Dense-reconstruction xKV is compute-bound: the normalized attention kernel speedup is below 1.0x in all settings and drops to ~0.4x at 122k. All headline latency/throughput gains come from the SR variants, so the paper's framing of the base method as reducing 'latency' should be more carefully qualified.

Per-task weaknesses are visible but under-discussed in the main text: on Llama-3.1, xKV's VT score (86.67) is notably below SnapKV/PyramidKV (~95), and the fixed key:value rank ratio (1:1.5) plus fixed per-task compression is acknowledged as suboptimal only in the appendix (D.3).

Baseline configurations are aligned by the authors but not all comparisons are at identical compression rates (e.g., xKV 8.03x vs PyramidKV/SnapKV 8x; MiniCache limited to 1.3x), and the MiniCache setup (merging half the layers) differs from its original configuration, so some head-to-head numbers should be interpreted with care.

The CKA-to-SVD-alignment argument (Appendix A) is an implication rather than a proof of cross-layer compressibility; the actual justification for the method's accuracy is empirical, which is acceptable but means the 'aligned singular vector' framing is partly interpretive.
Comparison with other post-training low-rank KV methods (e.g., Palu, LoRC) is limited to related-work discussion rather than direct experimental comparison on equal footing.

strengths: The motivating analysis is well executed: the contrast between low token-wise cosine similarity and high CKA scores across layers (Figure 2a/b), plus the rank-ratio analysis showing the required rank drops as more layers are grouped (Figure 2c), gives a clear, reproducible empirical foundation for the method.

The proposed method is simple, training-free, and practical: cross-layer SVD factorization (CLF) with a shared token basis is a natural but effective design, and the selective reconstruction variant (SR) addresses the compute bottleneck of dense reconstruction in a sensible way.

The evaluation is broad and mostly convincing: three model families plus an MLA/MoE model (Appendix E), RULER at 64K, LongBench, multi-turn NIAH, ablations over window size (Table 8), key/value-only compression (Figure 6), integration with quantization (Table 9), and real hardware throughput/latency measurements on an A100 with OOM comparisons (Figure 5).

The paper is transparent about the compute trade-off of dense reconstruction (normalized speedup below 1.0 at long contexts) and honestly scopes the limitation to long-prefill rather than long-generation settings (Section 7).
The broader CKA analysis across Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-4B, and the hybrid-attention GPT-OSS 120B (Appendix F) strengthens the generality of the core observation beyond a single model.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The core technique is essentially applying SVD jointly across a window of layers instead of per layer, combined with ShadowKV's existing landmark-guided selective reconstruction. The paper itself positions xKV-SR as 'extends' ShadowKV's system; the delta over prior art is a compression substrate change rather than a new mechanism.

The theoretical justification is overstated. The paper claims high CKA 'implies' aligned dominant singular vectors and repeatedly refers to 'see proof in Appendix A,' but Appendix A only shows that CKA is a singular-value-weighted average of subspace overlaps. High CKA does not strictly imply alignment of the top-k singular vectors, and no quantitative alignment metric (e.g., principal angles) is reported; the analysis is heuristic, not a proof.

Some headline claims do not fully match the reported numbers. The abstract claims 8x compression 'while preserving accuracy' and the conclusion claims accuracy 'within 2-3 percentage points' of the uncompressed baseline, yet Table 1 shows individual task drops up to ~7 points (e.g., FWE 85.42 -> 78.47 on Llama-3.1) and LongBench multi-doc QA drops from 44.72 to 38.82. Similarly, MiniCache's near-total collapse (45.04% avg at only 1.3x compression) appears inconsistent with results reported in the MiniCache paper, raising concern that the strongest inter-layer baseline was mis-configured or under-tuned.

Efficiency gains come only from the SR variants, which inherit the selective-attention machinery from ShadowKV. Plain xKV is actually slower than FlashAttention-2 dense attention, and even xK-SR shows 'almost matched' throughput versus ShadowKV with a slight shortfall (Section 5). The net contribution to the end-to-end system is narrower than the framing suggests.

Inconsistencies in reporting reduce confidence: Table 1's second block is labeled 'Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct-1M' while the text describes Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M; compression rates are computed 'by assuming a context length of 64k' rather than measured directly; and no error bars or seed variance are reported for any accuracy results.

Only prefill-side compression is addressed; generated tokens remain uncompressed, so the method does not apply to long-generation or reasoning-heavy workloads, which limits the practical scope of the contribution relative to its motivation around extended context usage.

strengths: The motivating analysis is a genuine contribution: the paper clearly demonstrates that token-wise cosine similarity across layers is low while CKA (subspace/geometry) alignment is high, and supports the CKA-to-singular-vector claim with a derivation in Appendix A. This reframing explains why interpolation-based merging (MiniCache) fails and motivates the method.

The proposed method is practical and well-engineered: training-free cross-layer SVD (CLF) with a shared token basis per window, a custom randomized SVD kernel with measured overhead (Tables 3-4), and a selective-reconstruction variant (xKV-SR) that keeps compressed keys and values on-GPU to bypass the PCIe bottleneck that limits ShadowKV.

Evaluation is broad and reasonably thorough: RULER at 64K, LongBench, multi-turn NIAH, three GQA models plus DeepSeek MLA (Appendix E), GPT-OSS hybrid attention (Appendix F), quantization integration (Table 9), window-size ablation (Table 8), key/value ablation (Figure 6), and detailed FLOPs/memory accounting (Appendix D.6).

The paper is commendably honest about trade-offs: it reports that dense reconstruction makes xKV compute-bound (kernel speedup < 1.0, dropping to ~0.4x at 122K), that xK-SR slightly underperforms ShadowKV in throughput at matched memory, and it includes a concrete limitations section (long-generation regime not addressed).
End-to-end system results (up to 4.23x throughput vs. full attention, OOM avoidance at large batch) demonstrate real practical value rather than only synthetic accuracy numbers.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the core operation is an SVD on horizontally concatenated caches of adjacent layers, and the selective-reconstruction pipeline (landmark construction, chunk selection) is adopted directly from ShadowKV. The contribution rests mainly on the cross-layer alignment observation and system integration rather than a new algorithmic technique.

The evidence for the headline accuracy claim is mixed. On Llama-3.1 RULER at ~8x compression, xKV (88.50) is slightly below SnapKV (89.68) and PyramidKV (89.94), so xKV 'closely matches' rather than surpasses token-eviction baselines there; the abstract's framing could overstate the gains. Some gains (e.g., +2.5% over ShadowKV* in Table 2) are modest relative to reported variance.

The CKA/singular-vector alignment study is primarily empirical and shown in detail only for Llama-3.1 in the main text; broader models appear only as heatmap figures in Appendix F without quantitative scores, rank statistics, or task variation, so the generality claim ('across diverse model scales') is somewhat under-supported.

Online SVD cost and memory at prefill are analyzed mainly in compute terms. Factorizing the concatenated W-layer cache requires materializing/handling very large matrices at 128K-256K contexts; the paper reports wall-clock overhead percentages but not peak-memory behavior of the decomposition itself, which matters for the claimed plug-and-play deployment.

Some experimental scope is narrow for the claims made: the multi-turn NIAH comparison (Figure 4) covers only Llama-3.1; rank ratios (1:1.5 key:value) and compression targets are somewhat ad hoc; and token budgets for SR baselines are fixed to 2K without sensitivity analysis.

Presentation has minor issues: an unclear/garbled code URL in the abstract, occasional typos ('enable effective information sharing', 'well-align basis', section cross-reference '(see § 3)' instead of §2.3), and compression-rate definitions differing between Tables 1 and 2 complicate cross-table comparison.
